claims.statement: Djimitflo has two independent Telegram surfaces with no shared transport code: the @djimitflo/telegram long-polling gateway (TelegramGatewayService in packages/telegram) and the single-bot webhook route at /api/telegram (createTelegramRoutes with TelegramBotService); both resolve Telegram senders to DjimFlo actors through an allowedUsers list plus an explicit userMap before any command runs.

The polling gateway starts only when operatorRuntime is true (runtimeProfileEnablesOperator: the operator or autonomous profile, never the default api profile) and only when TELEGRAM_BOTS_CONFIG is set; the JSON array's per-bot allowedUsers/userMap fall back to the TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS/TELEGRAM_USER_MAP parsers shared with the webhook route, TelegramGatewayService is dynamically imported from @djimitflo/telegram, and its ops are a TelegramApiService pointed at the loopback base http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}/api. Missing config or init failure logs and continues without blocking boot, and the instance is retained so the SIGTERM handler can stopAll() it to release the leases.

TelegramGatewayService serializes pollers with a per-token filesystem lease: the lock file is named by the first 16 hex chars of sha256(token) under DJIMIT_TELEGRAM_LEASE_DIR or os.tmpdir()/djimit-telegram-leases, created atomically with fs.openSync 'wx', carries a JSON payload of machineId/name/hostId/pid/startedAt, has a 2-minute TTL, and is kept fresh by a 30-second unref'd heartbeat that refreshes mtimes of all held leases.

On EEXIST the lease is reclaimed only through two tiers: a host-qualified dead-pid probe (same recorded host and process.kill(pid,0) raising ESRCH, with EPERM treated as alive so a live owner on the same host is never taken over and cross-host pid probes are skipped), or TTL expiry applied regardless of host or payload readability so a truncated lease from a crashed writer cannot wedge polling; an ENOENT between EEXIST and statSync is retried as a release race.

When lease acquisition fails, startAll retries with 2s/5s/15s/30s/60s backoff to ride out overlapping restarts and then skips that bot with a warning; per-bot init failure removes that bot's lease, and stopAll clears the heartbeat, settles every bot.stop(), and unlinks all held leases. The server retains the gateway and calls stopAll() in the SIGTERM handler specifically so a restart does not see EEXIST and skip polling forever.

A grammY middleware in the gateway enforces authorization before any command handler: the sender id must be present, be in the bot config's allowedUsers, and map through userMap to a non-blank actor string, otherwise the update is answered with '⛔ Telegram user is not authorized and linked to a DjimFlo account.' and dropped — the code comments that a bot token identifies the transport, never the requesting user.

Gateway commands are limited to /start, /status, /task <beschrijving>, /cancel <task_id>: /task forwards the prompt with the bot config's machineId to ops.createTask binding the task to that machine, /cancel without a wired cancelTask op surfaces TASK_CANCELLATION_UNAVAILABLE, and Telegram 409 getUpdates conflicts (another consumer of the same token) are handled in both bot.catch and the bot.start() rejection as warnings without crashing the process.

The /telegram prefix is mounted under /api with no mount-level middleware because the webhook authenticates itself via the secret header, and each diff handler self-authenticates at the '/' mount so a blanket guard would not intercept the public Telegram webhook.

POST /api/telegram/webhook fails closed before body handling: 503 when the bot is unconfigured, 503 when TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset, and 401 when the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header does not match; only then is the body passed to TelegramBotService.handleWebhook, returning {ok:true} on success and 500 on internal error.

parseTelegramAllowedUsers keeps only finite numbers from the comma-separated list, and parseTelegramUserMap accepts only a JSON object with all-digit string keys mapping to non-blank string user refs, returning {} on parse failure; TELEGRAM_USER_MAP can therefore reference DjimFlo users who must exist at configure time.

GET /api/telegram/status requires auth and returns telegramConfigStatus: configured/ready booleans, allowed_user_count, webhook_configured, linked_identity_count, approver_identity_count, a missing_env name list and a prose blocking list; since TG-2, ready requires the env half of the contract (TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, a non-empty allowed-user list, TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_URL, TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET) plus at least one telegram_identities row mapping an active user whose role holds approve:task (no database handle or a missing table counts as zero and fails closed), because buttons are authorised only by the D3 table; the serialized status never contains the token, secret, URL, mapped user refs or raw Telegram ids.

TelegramBotService resolves userMap entries at configure() time against users.id or users.email, and handleWebhook enforces a three-step identity ladder on chat messages before any command: sender in allowedUsers, sender linked to a DjimFlo user, and that account still is_active — each failure replies with a distinct refusal and no command executes.

Webhook commands split into read-only SQLite summaries (/status, /loops, /agents, /mission, /dennis — loop start/stop is deliberately not exposed) and mutations routed through an injected TelegramApiService (/task creates a pending local task on machine 'telegram-webhook', /cancel hits the task cancel route, /approve and /reject hit approval routes with SELF_APPROVAL_FORBIDDEN translated to a refusal, /dennis_task permission-checks create:task and creates a dry_run-only task pinned to dennis-agent); with no api injected every mutation answers TELEGRAM_API_UNAVAILABLE.

All outbound delivery (sendMessage and the broadcastAlert/requestApproval/requestTriage fan-out to the allowed users) posts MarkdownV2-escaped text to api.telegram.org/bot<token>/sendMessage with a 15-second timeout, skipping recipients already in progress.skip and tolerating per-recipient failures before throwing once at the end; every failure — including non-2xx Telegram rejections — is collapsed to TELEGRAM_DELIVERY_FAILED because the request URL embeds the bot credential and raw fetch errors must never reach logs or callers.

TelegramApiService is an authenticated API client rather than a task/approval writer: its constructor throws TELEGRAM_API_MUST_BE_LOCAL unless the base URL is http on 127.0.0.1/localhost/[::1] without embedded credentials so mapped-user Bearer tokens can never be forwarded remotely, requireActor resolves actors by id or email, rejects disabled or unlinked accounts (AUTH_DISABLED_OR_UNLINKED) and enforces RBAC (FORBIDDEN), and each request mints a fresh JWT for that actor with redirect:'error' and a 15-second timeout, surfacing the server's error code on non-2xx.

TelegramApiService's createTask/getStatus/cancelTask arrow-function fields are exactly the ops shape consumed by TelegramGatewayService: createTask posts a pending local-execution task tagged 'telegram' with the machineId in metadata and returns its id, getStatus counts visible active/pending tasks for that machineId, and cancelTask posts to /tasks/:id/cancel — so both Telegram surfaces funnel mutations into the same authenticated REST/approval spine.

The end-to-end chain test proves the ownership and governance invariants for Telegram-created work: an allowed sender's /task lands as a pending task owned and created_by the mapped user with a task.created audit event, the owner cannot self-approve (SELF_APPROVAL_FORBIDDEN), a viewer-role user gets FORBIDDEN, approval by an approver-role user lets mock execution complete, only the owner can cancel a running task, and unknown, unlinked, disabled, or downgraded senders create zero tasks.

The /telegram prefix mounts under /api with no mount-level middleware — the webhook authenticates itself so a blanket guard would break Telegram's calls — and the mount constructs its own TelegramApiService against the loopback base, so the webhook surface works whether or not the polling gateway runs; end-to-end tests prove the secret-gated webhook is reachable through the full router while neighbouring routes stay auth-protected.

POST /api/telegram/webhook fails closed at three gates before any body handling: bot not configured returns 503, an unset TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET returns 503, and an X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header that differs from the secret returns 401; only then does bot.handleWebhook() run, returning {ok:true} on success and 500 on internal error.

Approval and triage buttons are authorised by the D3 telegram_identities table, not TELEGRAM_USER_MAP: handleCallback requires allowlist membership plus mayApproveViaTelegram/mayActViaTelegram (an explicit telegram_identities row whose user is active and whose role holds approve:task, or write:governance for D5 pre-screen labels), refuses otherwise, and executes the decision through the normal approval/governance API routes as the mapped user — SELF_APPROVAL_FORBIDDEN and APPROVAL_ALREADY_PROCESSED are translated to operator-readable answers, and every allow or deny is recorded as a telegram_access judgment whose write failure never turns a deny into an allow.

The telegram_identities table (telegram user id to Djimitflo user, maintained only by an operator on /decisions) ships empty and is the sole source of who is behind a Telegram message for buttons and readiness: chat, group or bot membership grants nothing, and a viewer or inactive-user mapping never counts as an approver identity.

A configured webhook bot is registered with setPushSender and startOperatorDigest, becoming the operator-push channel: pushApproval, pushTriage, pushStall/pushNotice and maybeSendDigest deliver redacted text with inline buttons through the PushSender, dedupe per id with per-recipient delivery state in telegram_push_log/operator_digest_log, honor TELEGRAM_QUIET_HOURS and the TELEGRAM_PUSH_MAX_PER_HOUR cap, and retry failed or stale-pending deliveries on a 15-minute tick; TELEGRAM_PUSH_ENABLED, TELEGRAM_TRIAGE_ENABLED and the digest flags are all off by default and pinned to runbook documentation by a drift test.
